claim: Two-photon calcium imaging has created a unique opportunity to record the activity of large populations of neurons.
source: While two-photon calcium imaging has created a unique opportunity to record the activity of large populations of neurons, existing methods for inferring correlations from these data face several challenges.
evidence: This is a widely accepted statement in the neuroscience community about the capabilities of two-photon calcium imaging technology.

claim: Existing methods for inferring correlations from two-photon calcium imaging data face several challenges.
source: While two-photon calcium imaging has created a unique opportunity to record the activity of large populations of neurons, existing methods for inferring correlations from these data face several challenges.
evidence: The manuscript discusses these challenges in detail throughout the introduction and results sections.

claim: Observations of spiking activity produced by two-photon imaging are temporally blurred and noisy.
source: First, the observations of spiking activity produced by two-photon imaging are temporally blurred and noisy.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of two-photon calcium imaging observations.

claim: Inferring network-level features from binary spiking data is challenging due to the non-linear relation of neuronal spiking to endogenous and exogenous inputs.
source: Secondly, even if the spiking data were perfectly recovered via deconvolution, inferring network-level features from binary spiking data is a challenging task due to the non-linear relation of neuronal spiking to endogenous and exogenous inputs.
evidence: This is a fundamental challenge in computational neuroscience related to the complexity of neural dynamics.

claim: The proposed methodology explicitly models and directly estimates signal and noise correlations from two-photon fluorescence observations without requiring intermediate spike deconvolution.
source: In this work, we propose a methodology to explicitly model and directly estimate signal and noise correlations from two-photon fluorescence observations, without requiring intermediate spike deconvolution.
evidence: This is the main methodological contribution of the manuscript.

claim: The proposed estimator has theoretical guarantees on its performance.
source: We provide theoretical guarantees on the performance of the proposed estimator and demonstrate its utility through applications to simulated and experimentally recorded data from the mouse auditory cortex.
evidence: Theoretical analysis is provided in the manuscript, specifically in Theorem 1 and Appendix 2.

claim: The proposed method was applied to simulated and experimentally recorded data from the mouse auditory cortex.
source: We provide theoretical guarantees on the performance of the proposed estimator and demonstrate its utility through applications to simulated and experimentally recorded data from the mouse auditory cortex.
evidence: The manuscript presents multiple simulation studies and real data analyses from mouse auditory cortex.

claim: Neuronal activity correlations are essential in understanding how populations of neurons encode information.
source: Neuronal activity correlations are essential in understanding how populations of neurons encode information.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations in the manuscript.

claim: Correlations provide insights into the functional architecture and computations carried out by neuronal networks.
source: Correlations provide insights into the functional architecture and computations carried out by neuronal networks (Abbott and Dayan, 1999; Averbeck et al., 2006; Cohen and Kohn, 2011; Hansen et al., 2012; Kohn et al., 2016; Kohn and Smith, 2005; Lyamzin et al., 2015; Montijn et al., 2014; Smith and Sommer, 2013; Sompolinsky et al., 2001; Yatsenko et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: Neuronal activity correlations are often categorized into two groups: signal correlations and noise correlations.
source: Neuronal activity correlations are often categorized in two groups: signal correlations and noise correlations (Cohen and Kohn, 2011; Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Gawne and Richmond, 1993; Josić et al., 2009; Lyamzin et al., 2015; Vinci et al., 2016).
evidence: This categorization is supported by the cited references.

claim: Signal correlation quantifies the similarity of neural responses that are time-locked to a repeated stimulus across trials.
source: Given two neurons, signal correlation quantifies the similarity of neural responses that are time-locked to a repeated stimulus across trials, whereas noise correlation quantifies the stimulus-independent trial-to-trial variability shared by neural responses that are believed to arise from common latent inputs.
evidence: This is a standard definition in the field of systems neuroscience.

claim: Noise correlation quantifies the stimulus-independent trial-to-trial variability shared by neural responses that are believed to arise from common latent inputs.
source: Given two neurons, signal correlation quantifies the similarity of neural responses that are time-locked to a repeated stimulus across trials, whereas noise correlation quantifies the stimulus-independent trial-to-trial variability shared by neural responses that are believed to arise from common latent inputs.
evidence: This is a standard definition in the field of systems neuroscience.

claim: Two-photon calcium imaging has become increasingly popular in recent years to record in vivo neural activity simultaneously from hundreds of neurons.
source: Two-photon calcium imaging has become increasingly popular in recent years to record in vivo neural activity simultaneously from hundreds of neurons (Ahrens et al., 2013; Romano et al., 2017; Stosiek et al., 2003; Svoboda and Yasuda, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: Two-photon calcium imaging takes advantage of intracellular calcium flux mostly arising from spiking activity and captures calcium signaling in neurons in living animals using fluorescence microscopy.
source: This technology takes advantage of intracellular calcium flux mostly arising from spiking activity and captures calcium signaling in neurons in living animals using fluorescence microscopy.
evidence: This is a description of the basic principle of two-photon calcium imaging.

claim: The observed fluorescence traces of calcium concentrations are indirectly related to neuronal spiking activity.
source: The observed fluorescence traces of calcium concentrations, however, are indirectly related to neuronal spiking activity.
evidence: This is a well-known characteristic of calcium imaging data.

claim: Extracting spiking activity from fluorescence traces is a challenging signal deconvolution problem.
source: Extracting spiking activity from fluorescence traces is a challenging signal deconvolution problem and has been the focus of active research (Deneux et al., 2016; Friedrich et al., 2017; Grewe et al., 2010; Jewell et al., 2020; Jewell and Witten, 2018; Kazemipour et al., 2018; Pachitariu et al., 2018; Pnevmatikakis et al., 2016; Stringer and Pachitariu, 2019; Theis et al., 2016; Vogelstein et al., 2009; Vogelstein et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by the extensive list of cited references on spike deconvolution methods.

claim: The most commonly used approach to infer signal and noise correlations from two-photon data is to directly apply the classical definitions of correlations for firing rates to fluorescence traces.
source: The most commonly used approach to infer signal and noise correlations from two-photon data is to directly apply the classical definitions of correlations for firing rates (Lyamzin et al., 2015), to fluorescence traces (Fallani et al., 2015; Francis et al., 2018; Rothschild et al., 2010; Winkowski and Kanold, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: Fluorescence observations are noisy and blurred surrogates of spiking activity because of dependence on observation noise, calcium dynamics and the temporal properties of calcium indicators.
source: However, it is well known that fluorescence observations are noisy and blurred surrogates of spiking activity, because of dependence on observation noise, calcium dynamics and the temporal properties of calcium indicators.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of calcium imaging data.

claim: Due to temporal blurring, signal and noise correlation estimates from fluorescence traces are highly biased.
source: Due to temporal blurring, the resulting signal and noise correlation estimates are highly biased.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the temporal blurring in fluorescence observations.

claim: An alternative approach is to carry out the inference in a two-stage fashion: first, infer spikes using a deconvolution technique, and then compute firing rates and evaluate the correlations.
source: An alternative approach is to carry out the inference in a two-stage fashion: first, infer spikes using a deconvolution technique, and then compute firing rates and evaluate the correlations (Kerlin et al., 2019; Najafi et al., 2020; Ramesh et al., 2018; Soudry et al., 2015; Yatsenko et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: Two-stage estimates are highly sensitive to the accuracy of spike deconvolution.
source: These two-stage estimates are highly sensitive to the accuracy of spike deconvolution, and require high temporal resolution and signal-to-noise ratios (Lütcke et al., 2013; Pachitariu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references and is demonstrated in the manuscript's simulation studies.

claim: Deconvolution techniques are biased toward obtaining accurate first-order statistics (i.e. spike timings) via spatiotemporal priors, which may be detrimental to recovering second-order statistics (i.e. correlations).
source: Furthermore, these deconvolution techniques are biased toward obtaining accurate first-order statistics (i.e. spike timings) via spatiotemporal priors, which may be detrimental to recovering second-order statistics (i.e. correlations).
evidence: This is an inference based on the design objectives of spike deconvolution methods.

claim: Both direct fluorescence correlation and two-stage approaches undermine the non-linear dynamics of spiking activity as governed by stimuli, past activity and other latent processes.
source: Finally, both approaches also undermine the non-linear dynamics of spiking activity as governed by stimuli, past activity and other latent processes (Truccolo et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited reference and is a key motivation for the proposed method.

claim: Some existing studies aim at improving estimation of neuronal correlations but either do not consider signal correlations or aim at estimating surrogates of correlations from spikes such as the connectivity/coupling matrix.
source: There are a few existing studies that aim at improving estimation of neuronal correlations, but they either do not consider signal correlations (Rupasinghe and Babadi, 2020; Yatsenko et al., 2015), or aim at estimating surrogates of correlations from spikes such as the connectivity/coupling matrix (Aitchison et al., 2017; Mishchenko et al., 2011; Soudry et al., 2015; Keeley et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: The proposed methodology directly estimates both signal and noise correlations from two-photon imaging observations without requiring an intermediate step of spike deconvolution.
source: Here, we propose a methodology to directly estimate both signal and noise correlations from two-photon imaging observations, without requiring an intermediate step of spike deconvolution.
evidence: This is the main methodological contribution of the manuscript.

claim: The problem is posed under the commonly used experimental paradigm in which neuronal activity is recorded during trials of a repeated stimulus.
source: We pose the problem under the commonly used experimental paradigm in which neuronal activity is recorded during trials of a repeated stimulus.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup assumed by the proposed method.

claim: The proposed method avoids the need to perform spike deconvolution by integrating techniques from point processes and state-space modeling that explicitly relate the signal and noise correlations to the observed fluorescence traces in a multi-tier model.
source: We avoid the need to perform spike deconvolution by integrating techniques from point processes and state-space modeling that explicitly relate the signal and noise correlations to the observed fluorescence traces in a multi-tier model.
evidence: This describes the technical approach of the proposed method.

claim: Signal and noise correlations are cast within a parameter estimation setting in the proposed method.
source: Thus, we cast signal and noise correlations within a parameter estimation setting.
evidence: This describes the mathematical framework of the proposed method.

claim: The proposed solution method is based on variational inference, combining techniques from Pólya-Gamma augmentation and compressible state-space estimation.
source: To solve the resulting estimation problem in an efficient fashion, we develop a solution method based on variational inference (Jordan et al., 1999; Blei et al., 2017), by combining techniques from Pólya-Gamma augmentation (Polson et al., 2013) and compressible state-space estimation (Rauch et al., 1965; Kazemipour et al., 2018; Ba et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the technical approach of the proposed method, supported by the cited references.

claim: Theoretical guarantees on the bias and variance performance of the resulting estimator are provided.
source: We also provide theoretical guarantees on the bias and variance performance of the resulting estimator.
evidence: Theoretical analysis is provided in Theorem 1 and Appendix 2.

claim: The proposed method was applied to simulated and real data from the mouse auditory cortex during presentations of tones and acoustic noise.
source: We demonstrate the utility of our proposed estimation framework through application to simulated and real data from the mouse auditory cortex during presentations of tones and acoustic noise.
evidence: Multiple simulation studies and real data analyses are presented in the Results section.

claim: In application to repeated trials under spontaneous and stimulus-driven conditions within the same experiment, the proposed method reliably provides noise correlation structures that are invariant across the two conditions.
source: In application to repeated trials under spontaneous and stimulus-driven conditions within the same experiment, our method reliably provides noise correlation structures that are invariant across the two conditions.
evidence: This result is demonstrated in Real data study 2 and Figure 6.

claim: The joint analysis of signal and noise correlations corroborates existing hypotheses regarding the distinction between their structures.
source: In addition, our joint analysis of signal and noise correlations corroborates existing hypotheses regarding the distinction between their structures (Keeley et al., 2020; Rumyantsev et al., 2020; Bartolo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references and the results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Application of the proposed method to spatial analysis of signal and noise correlations in the mouse auditory cortex is consistent with existing work.
source: Moreover, while application of our proposed method to spatial analysis of signal and noise correlations in the mouse auditory cortex is consistent with existing work (Winkowski and Kanold, 2013), it reveals novel and distinct spatial trends in the correlation structure of layers 2/3 and 4.
evidence: This result is demonstrated in Real data study 3 and Figure 7, with comparison to Winkowski and Kanold, 2013.

claim: The proposed method reveals novel and distinct spatial trends in the correlation structure of layers 2/3 and 4 in the mouse auditory cortex.
source: Moreover, while application of our proposed method to spatial analysis of signal and noise correlations in the mouse auditory cortex is consistent with existing work (Winkowski and Kanold, 2013), it reveals novel and distinct spatial trends in the correlation structure of layers 2/3 and 4.
evidence: This result is demonstrated in Real data study 3 and Figure 7.

claim: The proposed method explicitly models the fluorescence observation process and the non-linearities involved in spiking activity through a multi-tier Bayesian forward model.
source: In summary, our method improves on existing work by: (1) explicitly modeling the fluorescence observation process and the non-linearities involved in spiking activity, as governed by both the stimulus and latent processes, through a multi-tier Bayesian forward model
evidence: This is a key feature of the proposed method described throughout the manuscript.

claim: The proposed method performs joint estimation of signal and noise correlations directly from two-photon fluorescence observations through an efficient iterative procedure, without requiring intermediate spike deconvolution.
source: (2) joint estimation of signal and noise correlations directly from two-photon fluorescence observations through an efficient iterative procedure, without requiring intermediate spike deconvolution
evidence: This is a key feature of the proposed method described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The proposed method provides theoretical guarantees on the performance of the proposed estimator.
source: (3) providing theoretical guarantees on the performance of the proposed estimator
evidence: Theoretical analysis is provided in Theorem 1 and Appendix 2.

claim: The proposed method gains access to closed-form posterior approximations, with low-complexity and iterative update rules and minimal dependence on training data.
source: (4) gaining access to closed-form posterior approximations, with low-complexity and iterative update rules and minimal dependence on training data.
evidence: This is a key feature of the proposed method described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The proposed method can be used as a robust and scalable alternative to existing approaches for extracting signal and noise correlations from two-photon imaging data.
source: Our proposed method can thus be used as a robust and scalable alternative to existing approaches for extracting signal and noise correlations from two-photon imaging data.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the simulation studies and real data analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: A MATLAB implementation of the proposed method has been archived in GitHub.
source: For the ease of reproducibility, we have archived a MATLAB implementation of our proposed method in GitHub (Rupasinghe, 2020) and have deposited the data used in this work in the Digital Repository at the University of Maryland (Rupasinghe et al., 2021).

source: For the ease of reproducibility, we have archived a MATLAB implementation of our proposed method in GitHub (Rupasinghe, 2020) and have deposited the data used in this work in the Digital Repository at the University of Maryland (Rupasinghe et al., 2021).

source: Our proposed method achieves the lowest NMSE compared to the others.

source: The leakage of our proposed estimates is the lowest of all four techniques, in estimating both the signal and noise correlations.

claim: The main sources of the observed performance gap between the proposed method and existing ones are the bias incurred by treating the fluorescence traces as spikes, low spiking rates, non-linearity of spike generation with respect to intrinsic and external covariates, and sensitivity to spike deconvolution.
source: The main sources of the observed performance gap between our proposed method and the existing ones are the bias incurred by treating the fluorescence traces as spikes, low spiking rates, non-linearity of spike generation with respect to intrinsic and external covariates, and sensitivity to spike deconvolution.

evidence: This is an explanation of the proposed method's advantages.

claim: The theoretical analysis corroborates that the explicit modeling of non-linearities results in robust performance under limited number of trials.
source: Our theoretical analysis in Theorem 1 corroborates that this virtue of our proposed methodology results in robust performance under limited number of trials.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by Theorem 1.

claim: The proposed method's analysis of the relationship between the signal and noise correlations in layers 2/3 and 4 in mouse A1 indicated a smaller correlation between signal and noise correlations than previously reported.
source: Our analysis of the relationship between the signal and noise correlations in layers 2/3 and 4 in mouse A1 indicated a smaller correlation between signal and noise correlations than previously reported (Winkowski and Kanold, 2013).
evidence: This result is shown in Figure 7A and 7B, compared to the cited reference.

claim: The proposed method suggests that the signal and noise correlations reflect distinct circuit mechanisms of sound processing in layers 2/3 vs 4.
source: Thus, our proposed method suggests that the signal and noise correlations reflect distinct circuit mechanisms of sound processing in layers 2/3 vs 4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The spatial distribution of signal correlations obtained by the proposed method was consistent with previous work showing significant negative trends with distance.
source: The spatial distribution of signal correlations obtained by our method was consistent with previous work showing significant negative trends with distance (Winkowski and Kanold, 2013).
evidence: This result is shown in Figure 7C and 7D, and is consistent with the cited reference.

claim: The proposed method revealed a significant negative trend of noise correlations with distance in layer 2/3, but not in layer 4, in contrast to the outcome of Pearson correlation analysis.
source: However, in addition, our proposed method revealed a significant negative trend of noise correlations with distance in layer 2/3, but not in layer 4, in contrast to the outcome of Pearson correlation analysis.
evidence: This result is shown in Figure 7C and 7D and Table 3.

claim: The lack of a negative trend in layer 4 could be attributed to the sparse nature of the noise correlation spread in layer 4.
source: The lack of a negative trend in layer 4 could be attributed to the sparse nature of the noise correlation spread in layer 4, as revealed by our analysis of two-dimensional spatial spreads.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The two-dimensional spatial spreads of signal and noise correlations obtained by the proposed method are more distinct than those obtained by Pearson correlations.
source: The two-dimensional spatial spreads of signal and noise correlations obtained by our method are more distinct than those obtained by Pearson correlations.
evidence: This result is shown in Figure 7E and 7F.

claim: The spatial spreads allude to directionality of the functional connectivity patterns, with a notable rostrocaudal preference in layer 4.
source: The spatial spreads also allude to directionality of the functional connectivity patterns, with a notable rostrocaudal preference in layer 4.
evidence: This result is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The proposed method can scale up favorably to larger populations of neurons, thanks to the underlying low-complexity variational updates in the inference procedure.
source: Our proposed method can scale up favorably to larger populations of neurons, thanks to the underlying low-complexity variational updates in the inference procedure.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulation study 2 with N=30 neurons.

claim: Due to its minimal dependence on training data, the proposed estimation framework is applicable to single-session analysis of two-photon data with limited number of trials and duration.
source: Due to its minimal dependence on training data, our estimation framework is also applicable to single-session analysis of two-photon data with limited number of trials and duration.
evidence: This is a stated advantage of the proposed method.

claim: A useful byproduct of the proposed framework is gaining access to approximate posterior densities in closed-form, which allows further statistical analyses such as construction of confidence intervals.
source: Another useful byproduct of the proposed framework is gaining access to approximate posterior densities in closed-form, which allows further statistical analyses such as construction of confidence intervals.
evidence: This is a stated advantage of the proposed method.

claim: A potential limitation of the proposed generative model is the assumption that there is at most one spiking event per time frame for each neuron.
source: A potential limitation of our proposed generative model is the assumption that there is at most one spiking event per time frame for each neuron, in light of the fact that typical two-photon imaging frame durations are in the range of 30–100 ms.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the proposed method.

claim: The Bernoulli assumption is relaxed in the inference framework by allowing the magnitude of putative spikes to be greater than one.
source: It is noteworthy that we relax this assumption in the inference framework by allowing the magnitude of putative spikes to be greater than one, thus alleviating the model mismatch during episodes of rapid increase in firing rate.
evidence: This is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In the regime of extremely low spiking rate and high observation noise, the proposed method may fail to capture the underlying correlations faithfully and its performance degrades to those of existing methods based on Pearson correlations.
source: Furthermore, in the regime of extremely low spiking rate and high observation noise, the proposed method may fail to capture the underlying correlations faithfully and its performance degrades to those of existing methods based on Pearson correlations, as we have shown through our simulation studies.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The proposed method addresses key limitations of conventional signal and noise correlation estimators that persist even in high spiking rate and high SNR conditions.
source: Nevertheless, our method addresses key limitations of conventional signal and noise correlation estimators that persist even in high spiking rate and high SNR conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated throughout the simulation studies and real data analyses.

claim: The proposed estimation framework can be used as groundwork for incorporating other notions of correlation such as the connected correlation function.
source: Our proposed estimation framework can be used as groundwork for incorporating other notions of correlation such as the connected correlation function (Martin et al., 2020), and to account for non-Gaussian and higher order structures arising from spatiotemporal interactions (Kadirvelu et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about potential future extensions of the method.

claim: Possible extensions of this work include leveraging variational inference beyond the mean-field regime.
source: Other possible extensions of this work include leveraging variational inference beyond the mean-field regime (Wang and Blei, 2013), extension to time-varying correlations that underlie rapid task-dependent dynamics, and extension to non-linear models such as those parameterized by neural networks (Aitchison et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about potential future extensions of the method.

claim: A MATLAB implementation of the proposed method as well as the data used in this work are made publicly available.
source: In the spirit of easing reproducibility, a MATLAB implementation of our proposed method as well as the data used in this work are made publicly available (Rupasinghe, 2020; Rupasinghe et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about data and code availability.

claim: All procedures were approved by the University of Maryland Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All procedures were approved by the University of Maryland Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Imaging experiments were performed on P60 and P83 female F1 offspring of the CBA/CaJ strain crossed with transgenic C57BL/6J-Tg(Thy1-GCaMP6s)GP4.3Dkim/J mice.
source: Imaging experiments were performed on a P60 (for real data study 1) and P83 (for real data study 2) female F1 offspring of the CBA/CaJ strain (The Jackson Laboratory; stock #000654) crossed with transgenic C57BL/6J-Tg(Thy1-GCaMP6s)GP4.3Dkim/J mice (The Jackson Laboratory; stock #024275) (CBAxThy1), and F1 (CBAxC57).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: The F1 generation of the crossed mice was used because they have good hearing into adulthood.
source: We used the F1 generation of the crossed mice because they have good hearing into adulthood (Frisina et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Cranial window implantation and two-photon imaging were performed as previously described.
source: We performed cranial window implantation and two-photon imaging as previously described in Francis et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Bowen et al., 2019.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: A cranial window of 3 mm in diameter was implanted over the left auditory cortex.
source: Briefly, we implanted a cranial window of 3 mm in diameter over the left auditory cortex.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.
